transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-03-04
- Time: 14:00 - 14:42 UTC
- Duration: 42 minutes
- Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE); Sofia Patel (Redwood SE); Marco Li (Redwood); Dana Reynolds (Lakeshore, Head of ML); Omar Aziz (Platform Eng); Priya Menon (Security); Caleb Ortiz (Product)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect): Dana and team are evaluating Redwood Dedicated for a production recommendation engine. Primary concerns: data isolation (VPC, encryption), predictable throughput for daytime peaks, burst capacity to handle marketing spikes, and a realistic rollout plan for 50-200 requests/sec w/ 2-4k token context. Next steps: pricing, security docs, benchmark run.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, I'll kick off, I'm Alex from Redwood, and with me is Sofia and Marco. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Dana Reynolds: Good, thanks. Appreciate you making time. We've got about 40 minutes, I think.
[00:11] Sofia Patel: Cool, we'll run through a quick discovery then get into sizing. Marco will cover performance and burst strategies.
[00:17] Omar Aziz: Quick note, Priya's on for security and Caleb is here for product questions.
[00:21] Alex Kim: Great. Dana, can you give us a 2-minute overview of what you're trying to achieve and what success looks like?
[00:28] Dana Reynolds: Sure, sure. We're building a personalized product recommendation engine that must serve both web and email channels. Right now it's a mixture of in-house inference on EC2 GPUs and some hosted APIs. We're seeing a ton of variance, like regular daytime troughs and then spikes during promo blasts. Success for us is predictable per-request latency under 200ms p50 for short completions, isolation of customer data, and cost that lets us stay within run rate targets. We're evaluating dedicated reserved GPU pools because ops wants to avoid noisy neighbor issues.
[00:54] Sofia Patel: When you say reserved GPU pools, are you thinking single-tenant hardware inside your VPC, or dedicated tenancy in our managed infra?
[01:02] Dana Reynolds: Prefer VPC-hosted, because of our compliance rules. But open to managed dedicated if we can guarantee network controls and logging.
[01:09] Priya Menon: To be clear, we need customer-managed VPC peering or private link. All model inputs are considered sensitive PII-ish, so KMS integration and audit logs are required.
[01:19] Marco Li: That's doable. Redwood Private supports customer-managed networking, and Dedicated offers VPC peering options with dedicated instances. We can lock down KMS/HSM integration and provide audit logs. We'll share the architecture diagram.
[01:30] Caleb Ortiz: On throughput — we're projecting average 60 rps during the day with bursts up to 250rps for a few minutes during promos. Each request is around 800 tokens. Is that realistic for dedicated?
[01:40] Sofia Patel: Good question. It depends on model and batching. For 800-token workloads, the dominant cost is the decode path; but with dedicated GPU pools we can set instance counts to hit throughput SLOs. For 250rps bursts, we'd recommend configuring reserved capacity for baseline and a burst buffer for short windows.
[01:54] Omar Aziz: How do you handle bursts? Auto-scale or pre-warmed capacity? We can't have cold-start latency of >2 seconds for some flows.
[02:03] Marco Li: Redwood Dedicated supports a couple of options: scheduled reserved nodes + an autoscale policy with fast warm-up using pre-warmed containers, plus a cold fallback to hosted models if capacity is exceeded. For the pre-warm we keep a minimal number of pre-initialized workers to reduce latency to sub-second for new requests. There's also a burst queue with graceful shedding or priority routing.
[02:25] Dana Reynolds: And what's the SLA if we exceed reserved capacity? We need predictable degradation behavior — like routing lower-priority requests to a lower-capacity quantized model and keeping critical flows alive.
[02:36] Sofia Patel: Exactly. We can set routing policies by route or token type. Critical routes get guaranteed capacity; background jobs can be routed to a quantized 4-bit model or queued. We can also do canary rollouts so you can test quantization profiles on a subset of traffic.
[02:50] Priya Menon: On the encryption side, we need end-to-end encryption at rest and in transit, and key access controls. Does Redwood support customer-managed KMS?
[02:58] Marco Li: Yes, we integrate with AWS KMS and HSM. For private deployments we can do customer-controlled keys; for managed dedicated we can set up a dedicated KMS key and restricted key policies. We'll include the security docs.
[03:08] Dana Reynolds: Great. A bit about timeline: procurement has a Q2 window, and infra needs to be ready for a pilot in May. Any reason that wouldn't be possible?
[03:17] Alex Kim: That timeline is reasonable. For Dedicated, typical onboarding is 6-8 weeks once legal and network are in place. If procurement moves quickly and we have the security checklist completed, a May pilot is doable.
[03:27] Caleb Ortiz: On sizing — can you walk through a sample sizing calc for 60rps baseline and 250rps bursts at 800 tokens?
[03:35] Marco Li: Sure. Quick back-of-envelope: assume model latencies on a single A100-like GPU at 800 tokens are say 80-150ms per request depending on batching. With continuous batching at the serving layer, you can get better throughput per GPU. For 60rps sustained, you'd need roughly 2-4 GPUs depending on model and batch size; for handling 250rps short bursts, we'd recommend a burst pool of additional GPUs or autoscale up to 8-10 GPUs for short periods. We'll propose multiple commitment tiers — baseline reserved count + burst buffer credits that let you burst above committed capacity for N minutes/month.
[04:09] Dana Reynolds: Does Redwood charge extra for burst minutes?
[04:12] Alex Kim: Typically yes — burst usage above committed capacity is billed at a higher overage rate or drawn from burst credits in a higher-commitment plan. We'll share a pricing sheet with tiered overage vs burst credits.
[04:24] Omar Aziz: About isolation: we need disk-level encryption and to ensure logs with PII don't land in shared logging buckets. Isolate telemetry and provide per-customer log retention controls.
[04:34] Marco Li: We can route logs to a customer-owned S3 via VPC endpoint or to a private logging collector. For disk encryption, we use customer-managed keys when required. We'll document retention windows and can support stripping logs of sensitive fields or redaction.
[04:47] Priya Menon: Also, are model artifacts stored on shared filesystem or per-tenant? We need to ensure model weights cannot be accessed cross-tenant.
[04:54] Sofia Patel: On Dedicated we provision model instances for your tenant; weights are stored in encrypted per-tenant storage. For Private on-prem we hand over the storage entirely.
[05:03] Dana Reynolds: Another concern is rollout: we want a canary to 5% of traffic then ramp. Can Redwood do per-route rollouts and automatic fallback?
[05:11] Marco Li: Yes, Redwood Console supports per-route model pinning, canary percentages, and automated fallback to a previous model or a hosted baseline if errors spike. We also have metrics for token-level cost and latency to help you observe regressions.
[05:24] Caleb Ortiz: For benchmarking, what do you need from us?
[05:29] Sofia Patel: We'll need a representative prompt set, sample input size distribution, request rate patterns (sustained vs bursts), and an API key or temporary access for the benchmarking environment. If you prefer, we can run the benchmark client in your VPC.
[05:41] Dana Reynolds: We'll prepare a 1k sample prompt set and a traffic trace for the last month. If you can run the benchmark in our test VPC that might be best.
[05:50] Alex Kim: Sounds good. We'll prepare a benchmark plan and share it.
[05:54] Omar Aziz: Let's talk about quantization and quality — we need to know expected regression for 4-bit vs fp16 so product can weigh cost vs quality.
[06:02] Marco Li: From our experiments, 4-bit symmetric quantization gives 5-10% quality shift on some tasks, less on straightforward classification. We recommend rolling quantized variants for background or low-priority routes first and keeping high-priority routes on higher-precision models. We'll include model-specific perf/quality tradeoff docs.
[06:20] Dana Reynolds: Will you support custom models we bring? We have an internally fine-tuned model for recs.
[06:25] Sofia Patel: Yes — Dedicated supports customer model onboarding. There are steps for validation, kernel compatibility, and weight format. We'll run an onboarding checklist. For private deployments, you can fully control model lifecycle.
[06:36] Priya Menon: Licensing and IP — if we upload models, what are Redwood's rights?
[06:41] Alex Kim: Standard practice: you retain model IP; Redwood has the right to operate the model for the service. We'll surface the exact contract language to legal.
[06:49] Dana Reynolds: Procurement-wise, who needs to be involved on your side?
[06:52] Alex Kim: I'll loop in our Sales Ops and Legal once you indicate intent; for advanced terms we'll involve our Security & Compliance team.
[06:59] Caleb Ortiz: Any limitations around regions? We need EU-residency for some data.
[07:04] Marco Li: We have regions in NA and EU; dedicated capacity can be provisioned in specific regions to meet residency requirements. For Private we can do on-prem.
[07:12] Omar Aziz: What about observability — token-level costs, per-route latency histograms?
[07:16] Sofia Patel: Redwood Console provides token-level cost breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and tracing hooks. You can export metrics to Prometheus/Grafana as well.
[07:26] Dana Reynolds: Okay let's do a quick recap and next steps.
[07:29] Alex Kim: Recap: we'll send pricing and commitment tiers, SOC2 and VPC deployment diagram, benchmark plan for running in your VPC, and a sample SOW for Dedicated onboarding. Action owners: Alex send pricing, Sofia prepare benchmark, Priya to reply with any initial security questionnaire items, Dana to share prompt set and traffic traces.
[07:50] Dana Reynolds: Yep that's right. Procurement window in Q2, pilot target May.
[07:55] Priya Menon: We'll get the questionnaire back to you. Thanks.
[07:58] Alex Kim: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up by end of week with docs and a proposed benchmark date.
[08:05] Dana Reynolds: Appreciate it, bye.

Notes about transcript quality: occasional speaker overlap, some words transcribed imperfectly (e.g., "KMS" was rendered as "K M S" in auto notes), timestamps approximate.
